MEPs want the EU to play a more active role in the East for internal reasons, such as the EU’s own security, as well as external ones, such as the security of the Eastern partners.
MEPs are divided between a “peace through speech” and a “peace through strength” vision for the EU, and that the EP’s role in foreign policy is limited but not irrelevant.

the EU’s role in the East and the EP’s views on this issue.
the question: what is the European Parliament’s view on the EU’s external security role in the Eastern neighbourhood?

the EP is in favour of the EU’s role of security provider in the East, but that this role should be limited to soft power tools.

the EP’s views are not coherent and are influenced by a number of different factors, including national, institutional, and personal ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the European Parliament is not only an actor in the process of the Europeanisation of security in the Eastern neighbourhood but also an active player in the process of security Europeanisation in general.
the European Parliament is not only an important player in EU external relations, but also an important player in the EU’s security policy.
the EP is a useful tool to understand the EU’s role in security, as it is the only institution in which the EU’s citizens are represented.

the EP has the potential to be a relevant actor in the EU’s external security, and that it is important for the EU’s foreign policy to take into account the views of the MEPs, especially in light of the EP’s increased competences in foreign affairs after the Lisbon Treaty.
the EU is not a security provider in its Eastern neighbourhood because of the EU’s lack of ambition, but rather because of the lack of ambition of its Member States.
